newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mahathir treats symptoms of Malaysia money politics.
newsitem.headline: Mahathir treats symptoms of Malaysia money politics.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has declared war on growing corruption in his political party, but a nexus between business and politics will make it difficult to eradicate, analysts said on Friday.
A tearful Mahathir warned delegates at the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) election assembly on Thursday that greed and "money politics" would destroy the 50-year-old party.

Mahathir has made money politics the battle cry of this four-day convention. He even ordered a blanket ban on campaigning for the 66 offices up for grabs to keep candidates from showering money and favours on delegates.

But outside the convention hall, almost all the cars in the VIP parking lot belonging to senior party officials were Mercedes Benzs, a testament to the wealth that comes with political power. Only one Malaysian-made Proton -- the national car that Mahathir has made the centrepiece of his industrialisation campaign -- could be seen.
"UMNO has come to be perceived as the key that opens the door to fabulous wealth and riches," said University of Sains Malaysia political scientist Chandra Muzaffar.
"A position of power or influence within the party hierarchy is seen as providing easy access to lucrative contracts, licences, shares, and the like," he told Reuters.
Candidates are said to have offered free trips, luxury hotel accommodation, lavish dinners and wads of cash to delegates, many of whom come from rural kampongs or villages.
The stakes were high even for posts at the branch level.

Last July, UMNO Secretary General and Information Minister Mohamed Rahmat caused a stir when he said a politician in southern Johor state was set to spend up to six million ringgit ($2.4 million) to get elected as a UMNO local chairman.
The money is usually raised from sympathetic businessmen, who would expect a quid pro quo in the form of licences or government contracts, political analysts said.
Mahathir hinted at this in his speech. "Where did all this money come from?...Perhaps rich supporters helped. But is this money free? Is this also not corruption?"

Chandra said money politics was "a symptom of an underlying disease in the way politics and business have become so deeply intertwined. That is why the umbilical cord that binds power to wealth has to be cut if money politics is to be checked".
Mahathir, a medical doctor by training, is treating the symptoms because that is all he really can do and because the "symptoms are causing quite a bit of pain", Chandra said.
Money politics was a relatively new phenomenon in UMNO, Mahathir said in his speech. In the old days, party members were not so keen to contest for posts.
Money politics gained impetus in the late 1980s when Malaysia embarked on an eight-year course of economic growth that created overnight millionaires in the Malay community.

Sanusi Junid, a former UMNO vice president and now chief minister of northern Kedah state, told reporters at the convention he thought money politics was a symptom of "culture shock" in the party "because too many people in UMNO became rich without having to work for it".
Malaysia's economic growth has been fuelled by a massive privatisation programme aimed at improving the lot of Malays, a majority of the population in an economy dominated by Chinese.

Some of the privatised entities were awarded to businesses linked to UMNO. Some were listed on the stock market and Malays were given preferential share allocations at bargain prices under a government programme.

International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz, who narrowly lost the leadership of the women's wing of the party this week, was fighting under a cloud of allegations that she had a conflict of interest in one share scheme.

Two other top UMNO officials who had to defend themselves against allegations of corruption and conflict of interest -- youth leader Rahim Tamby Chik and Youth and Sports Minister Muhyiddin Yassin -- also lost their races this week.
